title: Prediction: AMD Stock Could Double by 2028. Here's Why
author: Adam Spatacco
description: AMD is positioned to capture significant market share in AI accelerators with major contracts from Microsoft, Meta, OpenAI, and Anthropic providing multi-year revenue visibility. Wall Street projects AMD's revenue to grow from $50B in 2026 to over $100B by 2028, with EPS rising from $7.50 to $20. Even with P/E compression from current levels of 64 to 48-52, the stock could appreciate up to 101% by 2028.

insights.sentiment_reasoning: AMD has secured major multi-year contracts with leading tech companies (Microsoft, Meta, OpenAI, Anthropic), demonstrating competitive viability against Nvidia. Wall Street projects exceptional growth with revenue and EPS more than doubling by 2028 (50%+ CAGR). Even accounting for P/E multiple compression, analyst projections suggest up to 101% upside potential.
Microsoft is integrating AMD's Helios suite across Azure for AI workloads, indicating strategic commitment to AMD's technology and expanding AI infrastructure capabilities.
Meta committed to a multi-year deployment of up to 6 gigawatts of AMD Instinct GPUs, demonstrating confidence in AMD's AI accelerator technology for scaling operations.
While Nvidia maintains first-mover advantage in AI accelerators, AMD is increasingly capturing market share with high-profile wins, positioning itself as a credible alternative competitor.

title: Nvidia's Quiet Bet on AI Sandboxes Could Decide Who Wins the AI Agent Era
author: Beegee Alop
description: As AI agents begin executing code rather than just generating text, enterprises will need isolated sandbox environments to safely run generated code. This creates a new infrastructure market where Nvidia bets on faster cores, AMD on more cores per rack, Intel on existing x86 compatibility, and hyperscalers on custom silicon. The winner will be determined by which approach most efficiently completes agent tasks at scale.

insights.sentiment_reasoning: Nvidia is positioning its Vera CPU with 88 custom cores and 10-wide decode engines to handle agent execution workloads. The company is betting on faster, wider cores to complete blocking tasks quickly and plans to sell stand-alone Vera racks, creating a new revenue path beyond GPU systems.

AMD's Venice architecture supports up to 256 cores per socket and can scale beyond 36,000 cores per liquid-cooled rack. The company emphasizes compatibility with existing x86 tools and software, positioning itself as a practical choice for enterprises migrating agent workloads while maintaining architectural familiarity.

Intel's strategy relies on existing Xeon infrastructure familiarity and adding more cores through Xeon 6+ processors. However, the article suggests Intel faces challenges proving its existing workforce can compete on cost and performance, making its position more defensive than proactive in the emerging agent execution market.

Arm benefits from multiple competing Arm-based processors (Nvidia Vera, AWS Graviton, Microsoft Cobalt, Google Axion) gaining market share. As the instruction set blueprint supplier, Arm can monetize the market regardless of which specific processor dominates, creating a win-win scenario.

Amazon is preparing agent infrastructure through AWS Lambda MicroVMs and custom Graviton processors. As a hyperscaler controlling the entire workplace (hardware, software, services), Amazon can optimize total cost efficiency and potentially capture more value than merchant chip vendors.

Microsoft is adding isolated agent-execution environments to Azure and developing custom Cobalt processors. The company can integrate these with GitHub and enterprise software, giving it advantages in optimizing the complete workplace for agent execution.

Alphabet is preparing agent infrastructure through Google Cloud and developing custom Axion processors. Like other hyperscalers, Google can optimize the entire environment around agent execution, potentially lowering infrastructure costs and improving cloud margins.

title: Could AMD Dethrone Nvidia?
author: Catie Hogan
description: AMD is gaining ground in the AI chip market with major partnerships including deals with Anthropic, Microsoft Azure, OpenAI, and Meta, plus securing workloads from Turing. However, Nvidia still dominates with 80% market share and $75B in quarterly data center revenue compared to AMD's 5-7% market share. The article suggests both companies can grow substantially in the estimated $200B AI accelerator market by 2026, with AMD stock up 158% YTD versus Nvidia's 12% gain.

insights.sentiment_reasoning: AMD is securing major partnerships (Anthropic, Microsoft, OpenAI, Meta), developing competitive accelerators, gaining customer workloads from competitors, and showing strong stock performance (158% YTD). The company is successfully closing the gap in the AI accelerator market.

While Nvidia maintains dominant market position (80% share) and strong data center revenue ($75B quarterly), the article notes increased competitive pressure from AMD, stock underperformance (12% YTD), and potential for AMD to exceed performance in certain workloads. Position remains strong but facing headwinds.
Microsoft's Azure platform commitment to AMD's Helios rack-scale platform indicates diversification of AI chip suppliers and strengthened partnership, reducing dependency on single vendor.
Meta has existing partnership with AMD for AI accelerators, indicating vendor diversification strategy but no specific new developments mentioned in the article.

title: How Lisa Su Has Positioned AMD to Be a Big AI Winner and Why the Stock Is a Buy
author: Geoffrey Seiler
description: AMD CEO Lisa Su has strategically positioned the company as a major AI winner through major deals with OpenAI, Meta, Anthropic, and Microsoft for GPU deployments, innovative chiplet designs for inference workloads, and expansion into server CPUs. With agentic AI expected to shift GPU-to-CPU ratios and AMD targeting a $220 billion server CPU market with 50% market share, the company is positioned for significant growth.

insights.sentiment_reasoning: CEO Lisa Su has secured major partnerships with leading AI companies (OpenAI, Meta, Anthropic, Microsoft), positioned AMD's GPUs for the growing inference market, and expanded into high-margin server CPUs for agentic AI with ambitious market share targets.
Mentioned as the dominant competitor in AI chips; article frames AMD as emerging as a competitive alternative but does not provide specific negative or positive developments about Nvidia.
Signed a similar GPU partnership deal with AMD following OpenAI's commitment, validating AMD's AI infrastructure strategy.
Partnered with AMD to deploy Helios rack-scale solutions in data centers for inference, expanding AMD's presence in a major cloud provider's infrastructure.

title: Nvidia's Jensen Huang Confirmed Vera Rubin Chips Are Already in Production
author: Lyle Daly
description: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang dismissed reports of delays to the Vera Rubin AI chip platform, confirming that the chips are already in production with 'giant amounts of production incoming.' While SemiAnalysis had reported a 12+ month delay to the Kyber NVL144 rack-scale solution, Huang stated the reports are 'not true.' The confirmation is important given Vera Rubin's crucial role in Nvidia's forward earnings projections and the company's $1 trillion combined sales forecast for Blackwell and Vera Rubin through 2027.

insights.sentiment_reasoning: CEO's confirmation that Vera Rubin is in production with significant production volumes incoming addresses delay concerns and supports the company's critical earnings projections. The dismissal of delay reports and maintenance of product roadmap is bullish for investors, despite the stock being down 1.01% on the day.

Mentioned as a potential competitor that could gain market share if Nvidia experiences delays. However, with Huang's confirmation of no delays, AMD's competitive opportunity appears limited in the near term.
